title: Arnobii adversus nationes Libri VII
author: Arnobius of Sicca
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0034.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: ut ante milia annorum decem ab insula quae perhibetur Atlantica Neptuni, sicut Plato demonstrat, magna erumperet uis hominum et innumeras funditus deleret atque extingueret nationes, nos fuimus causa? ut inter Assyrios et Bactrianos Nino quondam Zoroastreque ductoribus non tantum ferro dimicaretur et uiribus, uerum etiam Magicis et Chaldaeorum ex reconditis disciplinis, inuidia nostra haec fuit?
passages.english: That ten thousand years ago a great host of men burst forth from the island which is called the Atlantic island of Neptune, as Plato shows, and utterly destroyed and wiped out countless nations, were we the cause? That between the Assyrians and the Bactrians, under the leadership of Ninus and Zoroaster in former times, the fight was waged not only with steel and strength but also with the magical and secret arts of the Chaldaeans, was this the result of ill will toward us?
passages.notes: 'inuidia nostra' could also mean 'our ill will' (i.e. ill will on our part); the sense in context is that the Christians are blamed.

passages.original: nonne uestrum quicumque est huic uel illi credit auctoribus ? non quod sibi persuaserit quis uerum dici ab altero uelut quadam fidei astipulatione tutatur? qui cunctarum rerum originem ignem esse dicit aut aquam, non Thaleti aut Heraclito credit? qui causam in numeris ponit, non Pythagorae Samio, non Archytae? qui animam diuidit et incorporales constituit formas, non Platoni Socratico? qui quintum elementum principalibus adplicat causis, non Aristoteli Peripateticorum patri? qui ignem minatur mundo, aduenerit cum tempus, arsurum, non Panaetio Chrysippo Zenoni?
passages.english: Does not each one of you believe this or that authority? Does not each man, by a kind of pledge of faith, guard what he has persuaded himself is being said truly by another? He who says that the origin of all things is fire or water, does he not believe Thales or Heraclitus? He who places the cause in numbers, does he not believe Pythagoras of Samos, does he not believe Archytas? He who divides the soul and posits incorporeal forms, does he not believe Plato the Socratic? He who adds a fifth element to the primary causes, does he not believe Aristotle, the father of the Peripatetics? He who threatens the world with fire, [saying] that it will burn when the time has come, does he not believe Panaetius, Chrysippus, Zeno?

passages.original: quod enim recte sit uinctum et nodis perfectissimis conligatum, dei bonitate seruari: neque ullo ab alio nisi ab eo qui uinxit et dissolui, si res poscat, et salutari iussione * donari. ergo si res est ita nec aliud conuenit uel existimare uel credere, quid animas admiramini mediae dici qualitatis a nobis, - cum, numinibus ipsis dicat Plato medias esse naturas, sed continuam et inocciduam uitam principali beniuolentia subrogari? si enim forte nescitis et antea uobis incognitum propter rei nouitatem fuit, accipite sero ac discite ab eo qui nouit et protulit in medium Christo, non esse animas regis maximi filias nec ab eo quemadmodum dicitur generates.
passages.english: For [he says] that what has been rightly bound and tied together with the most perfect knots is preserved by the goodness of God, and cannot be undone by anyone other than him who bound it, should the matter require it, and is granted [continued existence] by his saving command. So if the matter stands thus, and it is not fitting either to think or to believe otherwise, why are you amazed that souls are said by us to be of an intermediate quality, when Plato says that the very deities are of intermediate natures, but that a continuous and unending life is supplied to them by the goodwill of the supreme [being]? For if perhaps you do not know it, and it was unknown to you before because the matter is new, accept it late and learn it from him who knew it and brought it forth openly, Christ: that souls are not daughters of the supreme king, nor begotten by him, as is said.
passages.notes: The edition marks a lacuna (*) after "iussione"; the sense of "donari" there is uncertain. "neque ... et dissolui" is read as "cannot be undone". "generates" is taken as a misreading of "generatas". "protulit in medium Christo" is taken as "Christ", in apposition to "eo qui nouit"; the dative may be corrupt.

passages.original: uulgata. Aristoteles, ut Granius memorat, uir ingenio praepotens atque in doctrina praecipuus Mineruam esse Lunam probabilibus argumentis explicat et litterata auctoritate demonstrat. eandem hanc alii aetherium uerticem et summitatis ipsius esse summam dixerunt, memoriam nonnulli, unde ipsum nomen Minerua quasi quaedam Meminerua formatum est.
passages.english: [...] commonly known. Aristotle, as Granius records, a man of most powerful intellect and outstanding in learning, explains with plausible arguments and shows by learned authority that Minerva is the Moon. Others have said that this same [goddess] is the ethereal summit and the very height of the uppermost region; some [have said she is] memory, whence the very name Minerva was formed as if from a sort of 'Meminerva'.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence with 'uulgata' ('commonly known'), whose referent is lost.

passages.original: libet enim iam paucis etiam illas partes attingere, quibus alius aliud eadem de re dicere opinionum diuersitate monstramini. Ephorus has igitur numero esse tris effert, Mnaseas, quem diximus, quattuor, Myrtilus inducit septem, octo adseuerat Crates, ad extremum Hesiodus nouem cum nominibus prodit, dis caelum et sidera locupletans. nisi fallimur, ista dissensio nihil scientium uerum est, non ab rei ueritate descendens. nam si liquido sciretur quid sit, esset unanimis uox omnium et in eiusdem sententiae finem cunctorum pergeret et conueniret adsensio.
passages.english: For I wish now briefly to touch also on those parts in which you are shown, by the diversity of your opinions, to say one thing and another about the same matter. Ephorus, then, declares that they are three in number; Mnaseas, whom we have mentioned, four; Myrtilus brings in seven; Crates asserts eight; finally Hesiod sets forth nine with their names, enriching heaven and the stars with gods. Unless we are mistaken, this disagreement belongs to men who know nothing true, and does not come from the truth of the matter. For if what it is were clearly known, the voice of all would be unanimous, and the assent of everyone would proceed to and meet in the conclusion of one and the same opinion.
passages.notes: 'they' are the Muses (from the preceding context).

passages.original: ut enim de mediis conticiscamus auctoribus, aut ille primus eradit atque interficit sex diuas [Musas], si esse illas constat nouem, aut iste ultimus et extremus sex adponit, quae nullae sunt tribus solis in ueritate constantibus, ut neque sciri possit aut comprehendi, quaenam debeant addi, quae demi, et in periculum deducatur religionis ipsius susceptio, aut id quod non est colens aut quod sit fortasse praeteriens. Nouensiles Piso deos esse credit nouem in Sabinis apud Trebiam constitutos. hos Granius Musas putat consensum adcommodans Aelio, nouenarium numerum tradit Varro, quod in mouendis rebus potentissimus semper habeatur et maximus, nouitatum Cornificius praesides, quod curantibus his omnia nouitate integrentur et constent, deos nouem Manilius quibus solis Iuppiter potestatem iaciendi sui permiserit fulminis.
passages.english: For, to say nothing of the authorities in between, either the first one erases and kills off six goddesses [the Muses], if it is agreed that there are nine of them, or this last and latest one adds six who are nothing, since only three exist in truth; so that it cannot be known or grasped which ought to be added and which taken away, and the very undertaking of religion is brought into danger, either worshipping what does not exist or perhaps passing over what does. Piso believes that the Novensiles are nine gods established among the Sabines at Trebia. Granius thinks they are the Muses, giving his agreement to Aelius; Varro reports that the number nine [is meant], because in setting things in motion it is always held to be the most powerful and greatest; Cornificius [says they are] the guardians of novelties, because under their care all things are renewed and kept in being by novelty; Manilius [says they are] nine gods to whom alone Jupiter granted the power of hurling his thunderbolt.
passages.notes: The passage on the Muses is elliptical: 'the first one' and 'this last one' refer to authorities named before this excerpt, who gave the Muses as three or nine. 'Trebia' may be a corrupt place-name. The bracketed [Musas] is the edition's.

passages.original: nam quod nobis cateruas ignotorum alias inducitis deorum, existimare non possumus, utrumne istud serio atque ex rei compertae faciatis fide an fictionibus ludentes cassis ingeniorum lasciuiatis per luxum. quod abiectis infantibus pepercit lupa non mitis, Luperca, inquit, dea est auctore appellata Varrone. ex rerum ergo prouentu, non ex ui naturae dea ista est prodita? et postquam feros morsus immanis prohibuit belua, et ipsa esse occepit et ipsius nominis significantiam traxit? aut si fuit iamdudum dea, priusquam Romulus nasceretur et frater, cuius fuerit nominis atque appellationis expromite;
passages.english: For as to your bringing in other crowds of unknown gods, we cannot judge whether you do this in earnest and on the trustworthy basis of something ascertained, or whether you are playing with empty fictions and sporting wantonly in the extravagance of your wits. Because a she-wolf, not gentle by nature, spared the exposed infants, Luperca, he says, is a goddess, so named on the authority of Varro. So this goddess was brought forth from the outcome of events, not from the force of nature? And after the savage beast held back its fierce bites, did she both begin to exist and take on the meaning of her very name? Or if she was a goddess long before Romulus and his brother were born, tell us what her name and title were;

passages.original: numquid incestas nuptias cum sorore Iouem ipsum dicimus fecisse nos, aut in- Ii uitatum ad ius mensae pro suillis uisceribus prolem nescium Lycaoniam pransitasse ? numquid altero claudum. pede apud insulam Lemnum fabrilia opera exercuisse Vulcanum? numquid cupidinis atque auaritiae causa, sicut canit Boeotius Pindarus, Aesculapium fulminis transfixum esse telo ? numquid Apollinem ditem factum eos ipsos reges quorum gazis fuerat locupletatus et donis ambiguitate fefellisse responsi? numquid furem Mercurium publicauimus nos?
passages.english: Is it we who say that Jupiter himself contracted an incestuous marriage with his sister, or that, invited to a banquet in Lycaon's house, he unknowingly dined on [Lycaon's] offspring instead of pork innards? [Is it we who say] that Vulcan, lame in one foot, practised the smith's work on the island of Lemnos? That Aesculapius, as the Boeotian Pindar sings, was pierced by the bolt of a thunderbolt because of greed and avarice? That Apollo, having grown rich, deceived by the ambiguity of a response those very kings by whose treasures and gifts he had been enriched? Is it we who made public that Mercury is a thief?
passages.notes: 'in- Ii uitatum' is a scanning error for 'inuitatum'. 'prolem ... Lycaoniam' may mean Lycaon's son or child generally.

passages.original: neque enim potest infectum esse quod factum est aut rei gestae natura in alienam potest degenerare naturam. numquid bellum Iliacum in Socraticam uerti condemnationem potest, aut pugna illa Cannensis proscriptio fieri crudelitasque Syllana? potest quidem proscriptio, quemadmodum Tullius ludit, pugna dici appellarique Cannensis, sed quae gesta est dudum pugna, pugna esse non potest eademque proscriptio; neque enim quod gestum est potest aliud ut dixi quam id esse quod gestum est, aut in alienam migrare substantiam id quod in ui propria atque in sui generis qualitate defixum est.
passages.english: For what has been done cannot be undone, nor can the nature of a thing that has happened degenerate into a different nature. Can the Trojan War be turned into the condemnation of Socrates, or that battle of Cannae become the proscription and cruelty of Sulla? A proscription can indeed, as Tullius jests, be said and called a battle of Cannae; but a battle that was fought long ago cannot be a battle and at the same time a proscription. For what has been done cannot, as I have said, be anything other than what has been done, nor can that which is fixed in its own force and in the quality of its own kind pass over into a different substance.

passages.original: si humanam infirmitatem roges, nescio quid immane atque amplum: si deorum potentiam metiaris, successus quidam parui atque ut uerius eloquar genus angustissimum cauernarum paupertini cordis excogitatione suspensum. quorum si quaeris audire quis prior fuerit institutor, quis fabricator, aut Phoroneus, Aegyptius aut Merops tibi fuisse monstrabitur, aut ut tradit in Admirandis Varro, Iouis progenies Aeacus. sint ergo haec licet aut ex molibus marmoreis structa, laquearibus I I aut renideant aureis, splendeant hic gemmae I et sidereos euomant uariata interstinctione fulgores: terra sunt haec omnia et ex faece ultima uilioris materiae concreta.
passages.english: If you ask human weakness, [they are] something huge and grand; if you measure [them] by the power of the gods, [they are] certain small hollows and, to speak more truly, a most cramped kind of caverns, contrived by the invention of a paltry heart. If you wish to hear who was their first founder, who their builder, you will be shown that it was either Phoroneus, or Egyptian Merops, or, as Varro records in his Wonders (Admiranda), Aeacus, offspring of Jupiter. So granted that these are built of masses of marble, or gleam with golden panelled ceilings, that gems shine here and shoot out starry flashes in varied interspersion: all these are earth, and compacted from the lowest dregs of baser matter.
passages.notes: Stray 'I I' and 'I' in the text are scanning marks and are omitted. 'Aegyptius' could go with Phoroneus or Merops; taken with Merops. 'successus' is odd for 'hollows/recesses' (perhaps 'recessus').

passages.original: ubi denique Apollo diuinus, cum a piratis maritimisque praedonibus et spoliatus ita est et incensus, ut ex tot auri ponderibus quae infinita congesserant saecula ne unum quidem habuerit scripulum quo hirundinibus hospitium, Varro ut dicit set Menippeus, ostenderet? infiniti operis res est toto in orbe describere quae sint fana conuulsa terrae motibus et tempestatibus, quae incensa ab hostibus, quae ab regibus et tyrannis, quae antistites et sacerdotes et ipsi suspicione auersa nudauerint, quae ad ultimum fures et obserata pandentes † remedorum obscuritate † canacheni: quae tuta utique permanerent et nullis obnoxia fortuitis, si adessent dii praesides aut haberent aliquas templorum quemadmodum dicitur curas.
passages.english: Where, finally, was divine Apollo, when he was so stripped and burned by pirates and sea-robbers that out of all the weights of gold which countless ages had heaped up he did not have even a single scruple with which to offer hospitality to the swallows, as Varro the Menippean says? It would be an endless task to describe, across the whole world, which shrines were torn down by earthquakes and storms, which burned by enemies, which by kings and tyrants, which stripped by their own overseers and priests once suspicion had been turned aside, and finally which [were plundered by] thieves and those who open what is locked † ... †: shrines which would certainly have remained safe and exposed to no accidents, if the gods were present as protectors or had, as is said, any care for their temples.
passages.notes: 'remedorum obscuritate canacheni' is marked corrupt by the edition and cannot be translated with confidence; it apparently named a further class of plunderers. 'set Menippeus' read as 'Varro the Menippean' (author of the Menippean satires). 'auersa' in the priests' clause is uncertain in sense.

passages.original: ut communi uobis et simplici respondeamus uerbo, non scimus. quos enim uidimus numquam, qui sint scire quemadmodum possumus? ex uobis audire consueuimus deos esse quam plurimos et numinum in serie conputari: qui si sunt, ut dicitis, uspiam uerique, ut Terentius credit, eos esse consequitur sui consimiles nominis, id est tales quales eos uniuersi debere esse concipimus et nominis huius appellatione dicendos, quinimmo ut breuiter finiam, qualis dominus rerum est atque omnipotens ipse, quem dicere nos omnes deum scimus atque intellegimus uerum, cum ad eius nominis accessimus mentionem.
passages.english: To answer you with a common and simple word: we do not know. For how can we know who those are whom we have never seen? We are accustomed to hear from you that there are very many gods and that they are counted in the ranks of divinities. If they exist anywhere, as you say, and are true [gods], as Terentius believes, it follows that they are like their name, that is, such as we all conceive they ought to be and be called by the designation of this name; indeed, to put it briefly, such as is the Lord of things and Almighty himself, whom we all know and understand to be called the true God when we come to mention that name.
passages.notes: 'Terentius' is unclear; possibly Terentius Varro rather than the comic poet.
